decks.title: Surface Chemistry — Part 1: Adsorption
goals: Distinguish adsorption from absorption and name the adsorbate and adsorbent
Explain how the nature of the gas, surface area, pressure and temperature affect adsorption of gases on solids

slides.heading: Surface Chemistry
slides.body_md: Part 1 — adsorption: why molecules stick to surfaces. (This chapter is for formative assessment; it is not tested in the board exam.)

rows: Silica gel packet in a shoe box
Water vapour adsorbed on silica gel
Smoke settling in a chimney precipitator

visual.alt: Table of everyday examples of adsorption and colloids

slides.narration: Namaste! Surface chemistry is about what happens at the boundary between two phases, such as a gas touching a solid. The little silica gel packet in a new shoe box and the charcoal in a water filter both work because molecules stick to surfaces. In this part we study adsorption; in the next, colloids like milk, fog and ink. This chapter is assessed in school, not in the board exam.

slides.heading: Adsorption and absorption
slides.body_md: **Adsorption** is the accumulation of molecules at the **surface** of a solid or liquid, so their concentration there is higher than in the bulk. The substance adsorbed is the **adsorbate**; the surface is the **adsorbent**. In **absorption** the substance spreads **throughout** the bulk. Removing an adsorbed substance is **desorption**; when both happen together we say **sorption**.

rows: Higher at the surface than inside

visual.alt: Table comparing adsorption and absorption

slides.narration: Atoms at a surface are not surrounded on all sides, so they have unbalanced attractive forces. They attract molecules from the gas or liquid around them, and those molecules collect on the surface. This is adsorption. In absorption, as when a sponge soaks up water, the substance spreads through the whole material. Silica gel adsorbs water vapour, while anhydrous calcium chloride absorbs it.

slides.heading: Why adsorption is exothermic
slides.body_md: Adsorption lowers the residual surface forces, so it **releases heat**: $\Delta H$ is **negative**. The adsorbed molecules lose freedom of movement, so $\Delta S$ is also negative. For adsorption to be spontaneous ($\Delta G < 0$), the heat released must outweigh the entropy loss, i.e. $|\Delta H| > T|\Delta S|$. As adsorption proceeds, $|\Delta H|$ falls; when $\Delta H = T\Delta S$, equilibrium is reached.

rows: Molecules lose freedom on the surface

visual.alt: Table of the signs of enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy change for adsorption

math: \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S < 0 \quad\text{with } \Delta H < 0,\ \Delta S < 0
slides.narration: When a gas molecule settles on a surface, new attractions form and heat is given out, so the enthalpy change is negative. But the molecule also loses freedom to move, so the entropy change is negative too. Adsorption happens on its own only while the heat released outweighs the loss of entropy. As the surface fills up, less heat is released, and eventually the process reaches equilibrium.

slides.heading: Physisorption and chemisorption
slides.body_md: **Physisorption** (physical adsorption): weak **van der Waals** forces. **Chemisorption** (chemical adsorption): **chemical bonds** form between adsorbate and surface.

rows: N₂ on charcoal at low T

visual.alt: Table comparing physisorption and chemisorption

slides.narration: There are two kinds of adsorption. In physisorption, molecules are held by weak van der Waals forces, the same forces that hold liquids together. Little heat is released, the gas can be removed easily, and many layers can build up. In chemisorption, real chemical bonds form between the gas and the surface, so much more heat is released, the process is specific and hard to reverse, and only one layer forms.

slides.heading: Effect of temperature
slides.body_md: Physisorption, being exothermic and needing no activation, **decreases** as temperature rises (Le Chatelier). Chemisorption needs **activation energy**, so it first **increases** with temperature, then decreases at high temperature. A gas may be physisorbed at low temperature and chemisorbed at higher temperature.

visual.alt: Extent of adsorption against temperature: physisorption falls steadily as temperature rises, while chemisorption first rises to a maximum and then falls
visual.caption: Illustrative curves at constant pressure.

slides.narration: Look at how temperature changes the two kinds of adsorption. Physisorption gives out heat and needs no activation, so by Le Chatelier’s principle it falls steadily as the temperature rises. Chemisorption is like a chemical reaction: it needs activation energy, so at first it speeds up as the temperature rises, reaches a maximum, and then falls. Hydrogen, for example, is physisorbed on nickel at low temperature and chemisorbed when warmer.

slides.heading: Worked example: which kind of adsorption?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Classify each as physisorption or chemisorption: (a) the enthalpy of adsorption is $-25\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and the gas comes off when pressure is lowered; (b) oxygen on tungsten forms a single layer that can be removed only as tungsten oxide; (c) adsorption of a gas on charcoal decreases from 200 K to 300 K.

**(a)** Physisorption — low enthalpy, reversible.

**(b)** Chemisorption — a chemical bond (W–O) forms; one layer; irreversible.

**(c)** Physisorption — it falls as temperature rises.

visual.alt: Table of three cases, the clue in each and the type of adsorption

slides.narration: Use the clues in the table of differences. A small enthalpy of adsorption that is easily reversed points to physisorption. Oxygen that can only be removed from tungsten as an oxide must have formed chemical bonds, so that is chemisorption, and it forms just one layer. Adsorption that falls steadily on warming from low temperatures is physisorption.

slides.heading: Quick check: physisorption or chemisorption
slides.body_md: Pick the property that belongs to chemisorption.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the strength of the forces involved and how many layers can form.

slides.heading: Factors: nature of the gas and surface area
slides.body_md: **Nature of the gas:** in physisorption, gases that liquefy easily (high **critical temperature**) have stronger van der Waals forces and are adsorbed more. **Surface area:** finely divided or porous adsorbents (activated charcoal, silica gel, finely divided metals) adsorb more, because more surface is available.

visual.alt: Table of gases with their critical temperatures and the relative amount adsorbed on charcoal

slides.narration: Not all gases are adsorbed equally. In physisorption, gases that are easy to liquefy, such as sulfur dioxide and ammonia, have strong van der Waals attractions and are adsorbed much more than hydrogen or methane. A useful guide is the critical temperature: the higher it is, the more the gas is adsorbed. The adsorbent matters too: powdered or porous solids with huge surface areas, like activated charcoal, adsorb far more.

slides.heading: Effect of pressure: adsorption isotherms
slides.body_md: At constant temperature, the extent of adsorption $x/m$ (mass of gas $x$ adsorbed on mass $m$ of adsorbent) **increases with pressure**, steeply at first and then more slowly, approaching saturation. A curve of $x/m$ against $p$ at constant temperature is an **adsorption isotherm**. At higher temperature, less is adsorbed at every pressure.

visual.alt: Adsorption isotherms: the mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent rises steeply at low pressure and then more slowly; the curve for the higher temperature lies below the curve for the lower temperature
visual.caption: Illustrative Freundlich curves with 1/n = 0.5.

slides.narration: Raising the pressure of a gas pushes more of it onto the surface. At low pressure the amount adsorbed rises quickly; at higher pressure the surface begins to fill up, so it rises more slowly towards a limit. A graph of the amount adsorbed per gram against pressure, at a fixed temperature, is called an adsorption isotherm. The lower curve, at a higher temperature, shows that heating reduces physisorption.

slides.heading: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm
slides.body_md: Freundlich proposed an empirical relation for adsorption of a gas at constant temperature, where $k$ and $n$ depend on the gas, adsorbent and temperature, with $n > 1$. Taking logarithms gives a straight line: plotting $log (x/m)$ against $log p$ gives slope $1/n$ and intercept $log k$. It works over a limited range of pressure.

visual.alt: A straight line of log of x over m against log p, with a positive slope of one half and an intercept of log k on the vertical axis
visual.caption: Slope = 1/n; intercept = log k (illustrative: 1/n = 0.5, k = 1.2).

slides.narration: Freundlich found a simple equation that fits many isotherms: the amount adsorbed per gram equals a constant times the pressure raised to a power less than one. Taking logarithms turns this into a straight line. So if you plot the log of the amount adsorbed against the log of the pressure, the slope gives one over n, and the intercept gives the log of k. The equation works only over a limited range of pressure.

slides.heading: Worked example: using the Freundlich equation
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For adsorption of a gas on charcoal at 300 K, a plot of $\log (x/m)$ against $\log p$ is a straight line of slope $0.5$ and intercept $0.30$. Find $x/m$ at $p = 4\ \text{bar}$.

**Step 1.** Intercept $= \log k = 0.30$, so $k = 10^{0.30} = 2.0$.

**Step 2.** Slope $= 1/n = 0.5$.

**Step 3.** $x/m = k\,p^{1/n} = 2.0 \times 4^{0.5} = 2.0 \times 2 = 4.0$ (in the units of $k$, here g of gas per g of charcoal).

visual.alt: Table of the Freundlich constants and the calculated extent of adsorption

slides.narration: Read the two constants from the straight line. The intercept is the log of k, so k is ten to the power nought point three, which is about two. The slope is one over n, which is one half. Then put the pressure into the equation: two times the square root of four gives four. With straight-line data, Freundlich problems come down to reading slope and intercept carefully.

slides.heading: Quick check: the Freundlich plot
slides.body_md: Interpret the slope or intercept of a Freundlich plot.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember which constant comes from the slope and which from the intercept of the log plot.

slides.heading: Adsorption from solution
slides.body_md: Solids also adsorb solutes from solution. Activated charcoal shaken with ethanoic acid solution lowers its concentration; the extent of adsorption falls with temperature and rises with concentration and surface area, much as for gases.

rows: Ethanoic acid concentration falls after shaking with charcoal
Mg(OH)₂ precipitate turns blue with magneson dye
Dye adsorbed on the precipitate (a test for Mg²⁺)

visual.alt: Table of examples of adsorption from solution and their explanations

slides.narration: Adsorption is not limited to gases. If you shake charcoal with a solution of ethanoic acid and then filter it, titration shows that the acid concentration has fallen, because acid molecules have stuck to the charcoal. Sugar factories use charcoal to remove coloured impurities from raw sugar solution. Like gas adsorption, adsorption from solution increases with concentration and surface area and decreases with temperature.

slides.heading: Worked example: adsorption of ethanoic acid
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** $50.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.50\ \text{M}$ ethanoic acid is shaken with $2.0\ \text{g}$ of activated charcoal. After filtering, the concentration is $0.42\ \text{M}$. Find the mass of acid adsorbed per gram of charcoal ($M = 60$).

**Step 1.** Fall in concentration $= 0.50 - 0.42 = 0.08\ \text{M}$.

**Step 2.** Moles adsorbed $= 0.08 \times 0.0500 = 0.004\ \text{mol}$; mass $= 0.004 \times 60 = 0.24\ \text{g}$.

**Step 3.** $x/m = 0.24 \div 2.0 = 0.12\ \text{g per g}$.

visual.alt: Table of moles of acid before and after adsorption and the mass adsorbed per gram

slides.narration: The acid that disappears from the solution is the acid adsorbed on the charcoal. The concentration fell by nought point nought eight moles per litre in fifty millilitres, which is four thousandths of a mole. Multiplying by the molar mass gives nought point two four grams. Dividing by the two grams of charcoal gives nought point one two grams of acid adsorbed per gram of charcoal.

slides.heading: Applications of adsorption
slides.body_md: Adsorption is used to remove unwanted substances, to control humidity and in catalysis and analysis.

rows: Silica gel and alumina adsorb moisture
Reactants adsorbed on Fe, Ni, Pt surfaces (Haber process, hydrogenation of oils)
Ore particles adsorb pine oil and float

visual.alt: Table of applications of adsorption

slides.narration: Adsorption has many uses. Gas masks contain activated charcoal that traps poisonous gases. Silica gel keeps medicines and electronics dry. Charcoal removes colour from sugar solutions. Many industrial catalysts, like iron in the Haber process and nickel for hardening oils, work because reactant molecules are adsorbed on their surfaces. Chromatography separates mixtures because different substances are adsorbed to different extents.

slides.heading: Quick check: factors and applications
slides.body_md: Predict which gas is adsorbed most, or explain an application.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the link between how easily a gas liquefies and how strongly it is adsorbed.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Adsorption: surface accumulation; adsorbate and adsorbent; differs from absorption.
Exothermic (ΔH < 0) with ΔS < 0; spontaneous while |ΔH| > T|ΔS|.
Physisorption: van der Waals, low ΔH, reversible, multilayer, falls with T.
Chemisorption: chemical bonds, high ΔH, specific, one layer, rises then falls with T.
More adsorption with easily liquefied gases, larger surface area and higher pressure.
Freundlich: x/m = k p^(1/n); log plot slope 1/n, intercept log k.

visual.alt: Summary table of how factors affect physisorption

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Adsorption is the build-up of molecules on a surface and is exothermic. Physisorption uses weak forces and is reversible, while chemisorption forms chemical bonds and is specific. More gas is adsorbed when the gas liquefies easily, the surface area is large and the pressure is high. The Freundlich equation describes how adsorption depends on pressure.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Do not mix up adsorption (surface) and absorption (bulk).
Physisorption decreases with temperature; chemisorption first increases.
In the Freundlich log plot, slope = 1/n and intercept = log k.
Higher critical temperature → more physisorption.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: A few tips. Keep adsorption and absorption apart. Remember the opposite effects of temperature on the two kinds of adsorption at low temperatures. In Freundlich problems, the slope of the log plot is one over n, not n. And when comparing gases, the one with the higher critical temperature is adsorbed more.

decks.title: Surface Chemistry — Part 2: Colloids, emulsions and coagulation
goals: Distinguish true solutions, colloids and suspensions by particle size and properties
Classify colloids by phases and by the interaction between dispersed phase and medium (lyophilic and lyophobic)
Explain the Tyndall effect, Brownian movement, charge on sols, electrophoresis and coagulation (Hardy–Schulze rule)
Describe types of emulsions and everyday uses of colloids

slides.heading: Colloids
slides.body_md: Part 2 — mixtures between true solutions and suspensions.

visual.alt: Flow from true solution through colloid to suspension as particle size increases

slides.narration: Milk looks uniform, yet it is not a true solution, and it does not settle like muddy water either. It is a colloid, a mixture whose particles are bigger than ordinary molecules but too small to see or to settle. In this part we look at how colloids are classified, why they scatter light and carry charge, how they can be made to settle, and how emulsions such as milk and butter are built.

slides.heading: True solutions, colloids and suspensions
slides.body_md: The three kinds of mixture differ in **particle size**, which controls their properties.

visual.alt: Table comparing true solutions, colloids and suspensions

slides.narration: Particle size is the key. In a true solution, like salt in water, particles are smaller than about one nanometre. In a suspension, like sand in water, they are larger than about a thousand nanometres and settle out. Colloidal particles lie in between: they pass through filter paper and do not settle, but they cannot pass through a parchment membrane, and they scatter light.

slides.heading: Worked example: solution, colloid or suspension?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Classify each mixture and give one test that supports your answer: (a) copper sulfate solution; (b) dilute milk; (c) chalk powder shaken in water; (d) a sol whose particles are $50\ \text{nm}$ across.

**(a)** True solution — clear, passes through parchment, no Tyndall effect.

**(b)** Colloid (emulsion) — beam visible from the side (Tyndall), does not settle.

**(c)** Suspension — chalk settles on standing and is held back by filter paper.

**(d)** Colloid — particle size lies between 1 nm and 1000 nm.

visual.alt: Table classifying four mixtures with a supporting test for each

slides.narration: Use particle size and simple tests. Copper sulfate solution is clear and shows no beam, so it is a true solution. Dilute milk scatters a beam of light but does not settle, so it is a colloid. Chalk in water settles and is caught by filter paper, so it is a suspension. And particles fifty nanometres across fall within the colloidal range.

slides.heading: Dispersed phase and dispersion medium
slides.body_md: A colloid has a **dispersed phase** (the particles) spread in a **dispersion medium**. Either can be solid, liquid or gas (except gas in gas, which always forms a true solution), giving eight types.

visual.alt: Table of the eight types of colloid by dispersed phase and medium with examples

slides.narration: Every colloid has two parts: the dispersed phase, which is the tiny particles, and the dispersion medium they are spread through. Either can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. Solid in liquid gives a sol, such as paint. Liquid in liquid gives an emulsion, such as milk. Liquid in gas gives fog, and gas in liquid gives foam. Gases always mix completely, so there is no gas-in-gas colloid.

slides.heading: Lyophilic and lyophobic sols
slides.body_md: **Lyophilic** (solvent-loving) sols form directly by mixing (gum, starch, gelatin, proteins in water); they are **reversible** and **stable**. **Lyophobic** (solvent-hating) sols (metals, sulfides, hydroxides in water) need special methods to make; they are **irreversible** and are easily **coagulated** by a little electrolyte.

visual.alt: Table comparing lyophilic and lyophobic sols

slides.narration: Sols are also classified by how much the particles like the medium. Starch, gum and gelatin are attracted to water and dissolve to form lyophilic sols just by warming and stirring. These are stable, and if dried they re-form a sol when water is added. Metals and metal sulfides have little attraction for water, giving lyophobic sols. These must be made by special methods, cannot be re-formed once dried, and are destroyed by small amounts of salt.

slides.heading: Multimolecular, macromolecular and associated colloids
slides.body_md: **Multimolecular:** many small atoms or molecules aggregate to colloidal size (gold sol, sulfur sol). **Macromolecular:** single large molecules are already colloidal in size (starch, proteins, nylon in solution). **Associated colloids (micelles):** soaps and detergents behave as ordinary electrolytes at low concentration but form aggregates called **micelles** above the **critical micelle concentration** (CMC) and above the **Kraft temperature**.

visual.alt: Table of the three types of colloid by particle type with examples

slides.narration: Colloidal particles can be made in three ways. Many small atoms can cluster together, as in a gold sol. A single giant molecule, like starch or a protein, can already be large enough. And soap ions in water, above a certain concentration and temperature, gather into balls called micelles, with their oily tails inside and their charged heads facing the water. Micelles trap grease, which is how soap cleans.

slides.heading: Quick check: types of colloids
slides.body_md: Classify a mixture as a true solution, colloid or suspension, or name a colloid type.
slides.narration: Quick check. Use particle size and the names of the phases to decide.

slides.heading: Preparing and purifying colloids
slides.body_md: **Preparation:** chemical methods (double decomposition, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis), e.g. ferric chloride hydrolysed in boiling water; **Bredig’s arc** (metal sols); **peptisation** (a precipitate dispersed by a little electrolyte). **Purification:** **dialysis** removes dissolved ions through a parchment or cellophane membrane; electrodialysis speeds it up.

rows: FeCl₃ in boiling water → Fe(OH)₃ sol
Fresh Fe(OH)₃ precipitate + a little FeCl₃
Removes excess ions from a sol

visual.alt: Table of methods for preparing and purifying colloids with examples

slides.narration: Lyophobic sols are made by special methods. Adding ferric chloride drop by drop to boiling water hydrolyses it into a red-brown ferric hydroxide sol. An electric arc between metal wires under water gives a metal sol. A freshly formed precipitate can be broken up into a sol by shaking it with a little electrolyte, called peptisation. Excess ions are then removed by dialysis through a membrane that lets small ions pass but holds back colloidal particles.

slides.heading: Tyndall effect and Brownian movement
slides.body_md: Colloidal particles **scatter light**, so a beam passing through a sol is visible from the side: the **Tyndall effect**. Viewed under a microscope, the particles move in **zigzag paths** (**Brownian movement**) because molecules of the medium strike them unevenly; this helps keep sols from settling.

slides.narration: Shine a narrow beam of light through a true solution and you see nothing from the side. Through a sol, the beam shows up as a bright path, because the particles scatter light. This is the Tyndall effect, the same reason sunbeams show up in a dusty room or headlights in fog. Under a microscope, colloidal particles also jiggle about in zigzags, pushed by molecules of the liquid. This Brownian movement helps stop them settling.

slides.heading: Charge on colloidal particles
slides.body_md: Sol particles carry a **charge**, usually from **preferential adsorption** of ions common to the particle. All particles in a sol carry the **same** charge, so they repel and stay dispersed. A fixed layer of charge and a diffuse layer of opposite charge form an **electrical double layer**.

slides.narration: Colloidal particles are electrically charged. A ferric hydroxide sol made from ferric chloride adsorbs iron three plus ions and becomes positive; an arsenious sulfide sol adsorbs sulfide ions and becomes negative. Around the fixed charged layer is a looser layer of oppositely charged ions. Because every particle in a sol carries the same charge, the particles repel each other, which keeps the sol stable.

slides.heading: Positive and negative sols; electrophoresis
slides.body_md: Under an electric field, sol particles move towards the electrode of opposite charge: **electrophoresis**. This shows the sign of their charge.

visual.alt: Table listing common positive and negative sols

slides.narration: How do we know which way a sol is charged? In electrophoresis, a sol is placed in an electric field. Positively charged particles, such as ferric hydroxide, drift towards the negative electrode, and negatively charged particles, such as gold or arsenious sulfide, drift towards the positive electrode. When they reach the electrode, they lose their charge and settle out.

slides.heading: Quick check: charge and electrophoresis
slides.body_md: Predict the direction a sol moves or the sign of its charge.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which ions the particles adsorb from the solution in which they were made.

slides.heading: Coagulation and the Hardy–Schulze rule
slides.body_md: **Coagulation** (flocculation) is the settling of a sol when its charge is neutralised. It is caused by electrophoresis, by mixing two oppositely charged sols, by boiling, or by adding an **electrolyte**. **Hardy–Schulze rule:** the ion carrying charge **opposite** to the sol causes coagulation, and the **higher its charge, the greater its coagulating power**. The minimum concentration (millimoles per litre) of electrolyte needed to coagulate a sol in two hours is its **coagulation value**: the smaller the value, the greater the power.

visual.alt: Table of the Hardy–Schulze order of coagulating power for negative and positive sols

slides.narration: A sol stays dispersed only while its particles repel each other. Add an electrolyte, and ions of the opposite charge neutralise the particles, which then clump together and settle. This is coagulation. The Hardy and Schulze rule says that the ion with the opposite charge does the work, and the higher its charge, the more powerful it is. So aluminium ions coagulate a negative sol far better than sodium ions.

slides.heading: Worked example: comparing coagulating power
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Which of NaCl, BaCl₂ and AlCl₃ coagulates a negatively charged arsenious sulfide sol most effectively? (b) Arrange Na₂SO₄, Na₃PO₄ and NaCl in decreasing coagulating power for a positively charged ferric hydroxide sol.

**(a)** The cations act: Al³⁺ has the highest charge, so **AlCl₃** is most effective (smallest coagulation value).

**(b)** The anions act: PO₄³⁻ > SO₄²⁻ > Cl⁻, so **Na₃PO₄ > Na₂SO₄ > NaCl**.

visual.alt: Table of the effective ions and best coagulants for the two sols

slides.narration: First decide which ion matters: it is the one with the charge opposite to the sol. For a negative sol, look at the cations, and the aluminium ion with three positive charges wins. For a positive sol, look at the anions, and phosphate with three negative charges is most powerful, followed by sulfate and then chloride. The sodium ions in these salts do not matter for a positive sol.

slides.heading: Protecting lyophobic sols
slides.body_md: A **lyophilic** colloid added to a lyophobic sol forms a protective layer around its particles, so the sol is not easily coagulated. Such colloids are **protective colloids** (e.g. gelatin in ice cream, gum in ink).

rows: Ice cream (stops ice crystals and fat separating)

visual.alt: Table of protective colloids and their uses

slides.narration: Lyophobic sols are fragile, but they can be protected. If a lyophilic colloid such as gelatin or gum is added, it coats the particles with a solvated layer that shields them from electrolytes. That is why gelatin is added to ice cream, and gum to inks: they keep the fine particles from clumping together and settling out.

slides.heading: Emulsions
slides.body_md: An **emulsion** is a colloid of one liquid dispersed in another with which it does not mix. **Oil in water (O/W):** milk, vanishing cream. **Water in oil (W/O):** butter, cold cream. Emulsions separate unless an **emulsifying agent** is added: proteins and gums for O/W, long-chain alcohols and heavy-metal soaps for W/O. Soaps clean by emulsifying oily dirt into water.

visual.alt: Table of the two types of emulsion with examples and emulsifiers

slides.narration: An emulsion is one liquid spread as droplets through another that it does not mix with. In milk, tiny fat droplets are spread through water, so milk is an oil-in-water emulsion. In butter it is the other way round: water droplets in fat. Left alone, most emulsions separate into layers, so an emulsifying agent, such as the protein casein in milk, is needed to keep the droplets apart.

slides.heading: Colloids around us
slides.body_md: Many natural and industrial processes involve colloids.

rows: Scattering of light by dust and water droplets
Clay sol coagulated by salts in sea water
Alum stops bleeding from a cut
Al³⁺ coagulates the negatively charged blood colloid
Charged smoke particles neutralised at an electrode

visual.alt: Table of everyday phenomena and uses explained by colloid chemistry

slides.narration: Colloid chemistry explains many things around us. Where a river meets the sea, the salts in sea water coagulate clay particles carried by the river, building a delta. Alum stops bleeding from a small cut by coagulating blood. Cottrell precipitators in factory chimneys remove smoke by neutralising the charged particles on an electrode. And alum added to muddy water makes the clay settle, purifying it.

slides.body_md: Pick the most effective coagulant, or classify an emulsion.

rows: Charge is what stabilises lyophobic sols

visual.alt: Summary table of colloid properties and what each shows

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Colloids have particles between one and a thousand nanometres across. They are classified by their phases and by how much the particles like the medium. Colloidal particles scatter light, show Brownian movement and carry charge, which keeps lyophobic sols stable. Electrolytes neutralise that charge and cause coagulation, more strongly for highly charged ions. Emulsions are liquid-in-liquid colloids held together by emulsifiers.

For Hardy–Schulze questions, first identify the ion with charge opposite to the sol.
Smaller coagulation value = greater coagulating power.
Milk is O/W; butter is W/O.

Fog is an aerosol (liquid in gas)

slides.narration: Final tips. Always state particle sizes in nanometres. In coagulation questions, decide first which ion counts, then compare charges, and remember that a smaller coagulation value means a more powerful coagulant. Learn the phase names: fog is an aerosol and lather is a foam. Milk is oil in water, and butter is water in oil.

notes.title: Surface Chemistry — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Adsorption
sections.body_md:
**Adsorption:** accumulation of a substance (the **adsorbate**) at the surface of another (the **adsorbent**), so its concentration is higher at the surface than in the bulk. **Absorption:** uniform distribution throughout the bulk (water vapour in anhydrous CaCl₂). Removal of adsorbate: **desorption**. Both together: **sorption**.

Surface particles have unbalanced attractive forces, which adsorption partly satisfies, so adsorption is **exothermic** ($\Delta H < 0$). The adsorbate loses freedom, so $\Delta S < 0$. Adsorption is spontaneous ($\Delta G < 0$) while $|\Delta H| > T|\Delta S|$; it reaches equilibrium when $\Delta H = T\Delta S$.

key_terms.definition_md: The substance that collects on the surface.
The solid or liquid on whose surface adsorption occurs.
Removal of an adsorbed substance from a surface.

visual.alt: Table contrasting adsorption and absorption

sections.heading: 2. Physisorption and chemisorption
sections.body_md:
| Physisorption | Chemisorption |
|---|---|
| van der Waals forces | Chemical bonds |
| Low enthalpy, about 20–40 kJ mol⁻¹ | High enthalpy, about 80–240 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| Not specific | Highly specific |
| Reversible | Usually irreversible |
| Decreases with rise in temperature | Increases at first (needs activation energy), then decreases |
| Multimolecular layers | Unimolecular layer |
| More for easily liquefied gases (high critical temperature) | Depends on bond formation |

The same gas may be physisorbed at low temperature and chemisorbed at higher temperature (H₂ on Ni).

key_terms.definition_md: Adsorption by weak van der Waals forces; reversible and non-specific.
Adsorption by formation of chemical bonds with the surface; specific, one layer, needs activation energy.

visual.alt: Extent of adsorption against temperature: physisorption falls steadily as temperature rises, while chemisorption first rises to a maximum and then falls
visual.caption: Illustrative curves at constant pressure.

sections.heading: 3. Factors affecting adsorption of gases on solids; Freundlich isotherm
sections.body_md:
- **Nature of gas:** higher critical temperature → more physisorption (SO₂ > NH₃ > CO₂ > CH₄ > H₂ on charcoal).
- **Surface area:** finely divided, porous adsorbents (activated charcoal, silica gel) adsorb more.
- **Pressure:** at constant $T$, $x/m$ rises with $p$, steeply at first, then levels off (saturation).
- **Temperature:** physisorption falls with temperature (exothermic, Le Chatelier).

**Freundlich isotherm** (empirical, limited pressure range): $\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,p^{1/n}$, $n > 1$. Linear form: $\log \dfrac{x}{m} = \log k + \dfrac{1}{n}\log p$ — slope $1/n$, intercept $\log k$. For adsorption from solution, concentration $C$ replaces $p$.

**Applications:** gas masks (charcoal), humidity control (silica gel), decolourising sugar, heterogeneous catalysis (Fe in the Haber process, Ni in hydrogenation), high vacuum, chromatography, froth flotation, qualitative tests (magneson and Mg(OH)₂).

key_terms.definition_md: A graph of extent of adsorption against pressure (or concentration) at constant temperature.
The temperature above which a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone; higher values mean stronger physisorption.

visual.alt: Adsorption isotherms: the mass of gas adsorbed per gram of adsorbent rises steeply at low pressure and then more slowly; the curve for the higher temperature lies below the curve for the lower temperature
visual.caption: Illustrative Freundlich curves with 1/n = 0.5.

sections.heading: 4. Colloids: classification and preparation
sections.body_md:
**Particle size:** true solution < 1 nm; colloid 1–1000 nm; suspension > 1000 nm. Colloids pass through filter paper but not parchment; do not settle; scatter light.

**By phases** (dispersed phase in dispersion medium): sol (solid in liquid: paint), aerosol (solid or liquid in gas: smoke, fog), solid sol (coloured glass), emulsion (liquid in liquid: milk), gel (liquid in solid: cheese, jelly), foam (gas in liquid: lather), solid foam (pumice).

**By interaction:** **lyophilic** (starch, gum, gelatin — made by mixing, reversible, stable) vs **lyophobic** (metals, sulfides, hydroxides — special methods, irreversible, coagulated by a little electrolyte).

**By particle type:** multimolecular (gold, sulfur sols), macromolecular (starch, proteins), associated colloids (soap micelles above the **critical micelle concentration** and **Kraft temperature**).

**Preparation:** hydrolysis ($\ce{FeCl3 + 3H2O -> Fe(OH)3 + 3HCl}$ in boiling water), double decomposition (As₂S₃ sol), Bredig’s arc (metal sols), peptisation. **Purification:** dialysis, electrodialysis.

key_terms.definition_md: A sol in which the particles have strong affinity for the medium; reversible and stable.
A sol whose particles have little affinity for the medium; irreversible and easily coagulated.
An aggregate of soap or detergent ions formed above the critical micelle concentration.
Conversion of a fresh precipitate into a colloidal sol by shaking with a small amount of electrolyte.

visual.alt: Table of particle sizes of true solutions, colloids and suspensions

sections.heading: 5. Properties of colloids, coagulation and emulsions
sections.body_md:
- **Tyndall effect:** scattering of light by colloidal particles makes a beam visible from the side (seen when particles are much smaller than the wavelength yet large enough to scatter, and refractive indices differ).
- **Brownian movement:** zigzag motion from unequal bombardment by medium molecules; helps stability.
- **Charge:** from preferential adsorption of common ions; positive sols (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, Al₂O₃·xH₂O, methylene blue, haemoglobin) and negative sols (Au, Ag, As₂S₃, starch, clay). Same charge on all particles → repulsion → stability. **Electrophoresis** shows the sign.
- **Coagulation:** neutralisation of charge (by electrolytes, electrophoresis, oppositely charged sols, boiling). **Hardy–Schulze rule:** the ion with charge opposite to the sol coagulates it; coagulating power rises with that ion’s charge (for negative sols Al³⁺ > Ba²⁺ > Na⁺; for positive sols [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ > PO₄³⁻ > SO₄²⁻ > Cl⁻). **Coagulation value:** minimum millimoles per litre of electrolyte to coagulate a sol in two hours; smaller value = greater power.
- **Protective colloids:** lyophilic colloids shield lyophobic sols (gelatin in ice cream, gum in ink).
- **Emulsions:** O/W (milk, vanishing cream) and W/O (butter, cold cream); stabilised by emulsifiers (proteins, gums, soaps for O/W; long-chain alcohols, heavy-metal soaps for W/O).
- **Uses:** delta formation, alum to stop bleeding and purify water, Cottrell precipitator, blue sky, rain, soap cleaning.

Movement of colloidal particles towards the oppositely charged electrode in an electric field.
The coagulating power of an ion of charge opposite to the sol increases with the magnitude of its charge.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that adsorption is endothermic, or that physisorption increases with temperature.
- Taking the slope of the Freundlich log plot as n instead of 1/n.
- Choosing the ion with the same charge as the sol in coagulation questions.
- Saying a larger coagulation value means a stronger coagulant.
- Mixing up O/W (milk) and W/O (butter) emulsions, or fog (aerosol) and lather (foam).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a definition, a type of colloid, a coagulation order.
- Comparisons (2–3 marks): one mark per correct difference (physisorption vs chemisorption, lyophilic vs lyophobic).
- Calculations: Freundlich constants from a log plot; mass adsorbed per gram from a change in concentration.

questions.stem_md: Which property belongs to chemisorption but not to physisorption?

options.text_md: It forms only a single layer of adsorbate
It is caused by van der Waals forces
It decreases steadily as temperature rises
It is easily reversed by lowering the pressure

questions.solution_md: Chemical bonds form with surface atoms, so only one layer can be held — option (a). The other three describe physisorption.

questions.stem_md: In a Freundlich plot of $\log (x/m)$ against $\log p$, the slope of the straight line equals:
questions.solution_md: $\log (x/m) = \log k + (1/n)\log p$, so the slope is $1/n$ — option (d); $\log k$ is the intercept (b).

questions.stem_md: Equal volumes of four gases are passed over the same mass of activated charcoal at room temperature. Which gas is adsorbed most?
questions.solution_md: The most easily liquefied gas, with the highest critical temperature, has the strongest van der Waals attraction and is physisorbed most — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an example of absorption rather than adsorption?

options.text_md: Water vapour taken up by silica gel
A dye taken up on the surface of charcoal
Water vapour taken up by anhydrous calcium chloride
Hydrogen held on the surface of finely divided nickel

questions.solution_md: CaCl₂ takes water into its bulk (forming a hydrate) — option (c). The others are surface processes.

questions.stem_md: During adsorption of a gas on a solid, which statement about the changes in enthalpy (ΔH) and entropy (ΔS) is correct?

options.text_md: ΔH is positive and ΔS is negative
ΔH is negative and ΔS is negative
ΔH is negative and ΔS is positive
ΔH is positive and ΔS is positive

questions.solution_md: Attractions form (heat released) and the gas loses freedom on the surface — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gas is adsorbed on a metal. The extent of adsorption increases when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 450 K. The adsorption is most likely:

options.text_md: physisorption, which always increases with temperature
absorption into the bulk of the metal

questions.solution_md: Physisorption falls with temperature; an increase on warming shows an activated process, chemisorption — option (a).

questions.stem_md: At constant temperature, as the pressure of a gas over an adsorbent is increased to high values, the extent of adsorption x/m:

options.text_md: increases in direct proportion to pressure without limit
increases and then levels off towards a limiting value

questions.solution_md: More pressure pushes more gas onto the surface until it is nearly saturated — option (d).

questions.stem_md: One gram of charcoal is used as a single lump, and another gram is ground into a fine powder. The powder adsorbs much more gas because:

options.text_md: its surface area is much larger
powdered charcoal forms chemical bonds with every gas

questions.solution_md: Adsorption is a surface phenomenon, so more surface per gram means more adsorption — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the hardening of vegetable oils, hydrogen is passed through hot oil containing finely divided nickel. The role of adsorption here is that:

options.text_md: nickel absorbs all the oil into its bulk
hydrogen and oil molecules are adsorbed on the nickel surface, where they react more easily
nickel adsorbs water and removes it from the oil
adsorption raises the activation energy of the reaction

questions.solution_md: In heterogeneous catalysis, reactants are adsorbed on the catalyst surface, which weakens bonds and brings them together — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Physisorption of a gas on charcoal increases when the temperature is raised.
questions.solution_md: False. Physisorption is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier’s principle it decreases as temperature rises.

questions.stem_md: The substance that accumulates on a surface during adsorption is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: The **adsorbate**; the surface is the adsorbent.

questions.stem_md: Match each application with the adsorbent used.
questions.solution_md: Gas mask → charcoal; drying → silica gel; Haber → iron; hydrogenation → nickel.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Chemisorption is highly specific.

**Reason (R):** Chemisorption takes place only if chemical bonds can form between the adsorbate and the adsorbent.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the need to form bonds explains the specificity (e.g. O₂ chemisorbs on metals but not on noble gases) — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Physisorption decreases with increase in temperature.

**Reason (R):** Physisorption is an endothermic process.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — physisorption is exothermic, which is why heating reduces it — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ammonia is adsorbed on charcoal much more than hydrogen at room temperature.

**Reason (R):** Hydrogen molecules are smaller than ammonia molecules.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but size is not the reason: ammonia has a much higher critical temperature (stronger van der Waals forces) — option (b).

questions.stem_md: For the adsorption of a gas on charcoal at 300 K, a plot of $\log (x/m)$ against $\log p$ is a straight line with slope $0.25$ and intercept $0.48$. Using $k = 10^{0.48} = 3.0$, find $x/m$, in g of gas per g of charcoal, at $p = 16\ \text{bar}$.
The Freundlich plot for adsorption of a gas has a slope of $0.40$. What is the value of $n$?

$100\ \text{mL}$ of $0.60\ \text{M}$ ethanoic acid ($M = 60$) is shaken with $3.0\ \text{g}$ of activated charcoal. After filtering, the acid concentration is $0.45\ \text{M}$. What mass of acid, in grams, is adsorbed per gram of charcoal?
questions.solution_md: Fall $= 0.60 - 0.45 = 0.15\ \text{M}$; moles adsorbed $= 0.15 \times 0.100 = 0.015$; mass $= 0.015 \times 60 = 0.90\ \text{g}$; per gram $= 0.90 \div 3.0 = 0.30$, so $0.30$ g per g.

questions.stem_md: For a gas obeying the Freundlich isotherm with $1/n = 0.5$, by what factor does $x/m$ increase when the pressure is increased from $2$ bar to $8$ bar at constant temperature?
Explain why adsorption is always exothermic, and why it stops increasing after some time even though gas is still present.

answer.model_answer_md: Surface particles have unbalanced attractive forces; when gas molecules are adsorbed, attractions form and energy is released as heat, so adsorption is exothermic. As the surface fills, less heat is released per molecule while the entropy loss continues; when ΔH becomes equal to TΔS, ΔG becomes zero and equilibrium is reached.

questions.solution_md: Residual forces satisfied; equilibrium when ΔH = TΔS.

marking_scheme.step: Residual surface forces satisfied, heat released

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between physisorption and chemisorption.

answer.model_answer_md: Physisorption is caused by weak van der Waals forces, while chemisorption involves the formation of chemical bonds between adsorbate and surface. The enthalpy of physisorption is low (about 20–40 kJ mol⁻¹), while that of chemisorption is high (about 80–240 kJ mol⁻¹). Physisorption is reversible, non-specific and forms several layers, while chemisorption is usually irreversible, specific and forms a single layer.

questions.solution_md: Forces, enthalpy, reversibility/specificity/layers.

questions.stem_md: A student wants to show that charcoal adsorbs ethanoic acid from solution. Describe what she should do and what result she should expect.

answer.model_answer_md: She should titrate a known volume of ethanoic acid solution with standard NaOH, shake an equal volume of the same solution with a weighed amount of activated charcoal, filter, and titrate the filtrate in the same way. The filtrate needs less alkali, showing that the acid concentration has fallen because acid was adsorbed on the charcoal.

questions.solution_md: Titrate before and after shaking with charcoal.

marking_scheme.step: Titration before and after shaking with charcoal

questions.stem_md: Explain why (a) a small packet of silica gel is kept in a new camera bag, and (b) a gas is adsorbed more on charcoal cooled with liquid nitrogen than at room temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Silica gel has a very large surface area and adsorbs water vapour, keeping the air in the bag dry so the camera does not get damp or mouldy. (b) Physisorption is exothermic, so cooling shifts the equilibrium towards adsorption and more gas is held.

questions.solution_md: Moisture adsorption; exothermic physisorption favoured at low temperature.

questions.stem_md: Hydrogen and sulfur dioxide are each passed over powdered charcoal at room temperature, first at 1 bar and then at 5 bar. Predict which gas is adsorbed more and how raising the pressure affects each, giving reasons. How would warming the charcoal change the results?

answer.model_answer_md: Sulfur dioxide is adsorbed far more, because it is easily liquefied (high critical temperature) and so has much stronger van der Waals attractions to the charcoal than hydrogen. Raising the pressure from 1 to 5 bar increases the amount of each gas adsorbed, though not in direct proportion, as described by the Freundlich isotherm. Warming the charcoal decreases the adsorption of both gases, because physisorption is exothermic.

questions.solution_md: SO₂ more (critical temperature); more with pressure; less on warming.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between adsorption and absorption with an example of each.

(b) Explain, using ΔH and ΔS, why adsorption is spontaneous at first and then reaches equilibrium.

(c) State the Freundlich adsorption isotherm and explain how its constants can be found from experimental data.

answer.model_answer_md: In adsorption a substance collects only at the surface, for example water vapour on silica gel; in absorption it spreads uniformly through the bulk, as water vapour in anhydrous calcium chloride. Adsorption releases heat, so ΔH is negative, but the adsorbed molecules lose freedom, so ΔS is negative. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative while |ΔH| exceeds T|ΔS|, so adsorption is spontaneous at first. As the surface fills, |ΔH| falls; when ΔH = TΔS, ΔG = 0 and equilibrium is reached. Freundlich proposed x/m = k p^(1/n), with n greater than 1, at constant temperature. Taking logarithms, log(x/m) = log k + (1/n) log p. Plotting log(x/m) against log p gives a straight line whose slope is 1/n and whose intercept is log k.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; ΔH, ΔS, ΔG; Freundlich and log plot.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Signs of ΔH and ΔS and spontaneity

questions.stem_md:
(a) Compare physisorption and chemisorption under four headings.

(b) Sketch and explain how the extent of each varies with temperature.

(c) Explain the role of adsorption in heterogeneous catalysis with one example.

answer.model_answer_md: Physisorption involves van der Waals forces, has a low enthalpy (20–40 kJ mol⁻¹), is reversible and non-specific, and forms multimolecular layers. Chemisorption involves chemical bonds, has a high enthalpy (80–240 kJ mol⁻¹), is usually irreversible and specific, and forms one layer. The extent of physisorption falls steadily with rising temperature because it is exothermic. Chemisorption needs activation energy, so its extent first rises with temperature to a maximum and then falls. In heterogeneous catalysis, reactant molecules are adsorbed on the catalyst surface, which raises their concentration there and weakens their bonds, lowering the activation energy. For example, in the Haber process nitrogen and hydrogen are adsorbed on iron, react, and ammonia desorbs.

questions.solution_md: Comparison; temperature graphs; catalysis.

questions.stem_md: Fog is a colloid in which:

options.text_md: gas bubbles are dispersed in a liquid (a foam)
a liquid is dispersed in a solid (a gel)
liquid droplets are dispersed in a gas (an aerosol)
solid particles are dispersed in a liquid (a sol)

questions.solution_md: Fog is water droplets in air — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A ferric hydroxide sol is made by adding ferric chloride to boiling water. When an electric field is applied, the sol particles move towards:

options.text_md: the anode, because they adsorb Cl⁻ ions and are negatively charged
neither electrode, because colloidal particles are neutral
both electrodes equally, because of Brownian movement
the cathode, because they adsorb Fe³⁺ ions and are positively charged

questions.solution_md: The particles preferentially adsorb Fe³⁺ (an ion common to them), so they are positive and move to the negative electrode — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which electrolyte coagulates a negatively charged arsenious sulfide sol most effectively?
questions.solution_md: For a negative sol the cation acts; Al³⁺ has the highest charge (Hardy–Schulze rule) — option (b). Na₃PO₄ supplies only Na⁺ as cation (d).

questions.stem_md: A mixture passes through filter paper but not through a parchment membrane, does not settle on standing, and shows the Tyndall effect. Its particles are most likely in the size range:
questions.solution_md: These are the properties of a colloid — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these forms a lyophilic sol in water?
questions.solution_md: Starch has a strong affinity for water and forms a sol on warming — option (d). The others form lyophobic sols.

questions.stem_md: Butter is an example of:
questions.solution_md: In butter, water droplets are dispersed in fat — option (a). Milk is oil-in-water (b).

questions.stem_md: Headlight beams are clearly visible on a foggy night but hardly visible on a clear night. This is because:

options.text_md: fog droplets of colloidal size scatter the light (Tyndall effect)
air molecules on a clear night are larger than fog droplets

questions.solution_md: Colloidal droplets scatter light, making the beam path visible — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which sol is positively charged?
questions.solution_md: Basic dyes such as methylene blue, and hydrated metal oxides, form positive sols — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which anion has the greatest coagulating power for a positively charged ferric hydroxide sol?
questions.solution_md: For a positive sol the anion acts; the highest charge, 4−, is most powerful — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A barber rubs a block of alum on a small cut to stop the bleeding. Alum works because:

options.text_md: Al³⁺ ions coagulate the negatively charged colloidal particles in blood
alum adsorbs all the water in blood
sulfate ions coagulate positively charged blood particles
alum forms an emulsion with blood

questions.solution_md: Blood is a negatively charged colloid; the highly charged Al³⁺ ion coagulates it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Deltas form where rivers meet the sea. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: sea water is denser, so clay floats on it
clay particles dissolve in sea water
salts in sea water coagulate the charged clay particles carried by the river

questions.solution_md: River water carries a clay sol; electrolytes in sea water neutralise its charge and it settles — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A freshly prepared ferric hydroxide sol contains excess HCl. The best way to remove it is:

options.text_md: dialysis through a cellophane bag placed in running water

questions.solution_md: Small ions pass through the membrane but colloidal particles do not — option (c). Filter paper lets both through (a); electrolyte or boiling would coagulate the sol.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Soap forms micelles in water at all concentrations and temperatures.
questions.solution_md: False. Micelles form only above the critical micelle concentration (CMC) and above the Kraft temperature.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A lyophobic sol, once coagulated and dried, re-forms a sol simply on adding the dispersion medium.
questions.solution_md: False. Lyophobic sols are irreversible; it is lyophilic sols that re-form on adding the medium.

questions.stem_md: A torch beam shone through a glass of diluted milk shows up as a bright path when seen from the side, but not through a glass of salt water. This is the ___ effect.
questions.solution_md: The **Tyndall** effect: milk droplets are of colloidal size and scatter light; dissolved ions are too small.

questions.stem_md: Converting a freshly prepared precipitate into a colloidal sol by shaking it with a small amount of an electrolyte is called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Peptisation**.

questions.stem_md: Match each everyday material with its type of colloid.
questions.solution_md: Lather → foam; cheese → gel; smoke → aerosol; pumice → solid foam.

questions.stem_md: Match each observation with the property of colloids it illustrates.

options.text_md: Sunbeam visible in a dusty room
Particles seen jiggling under a microscope
Sol particles drifting to an electrode
Clay settling where a river meets the sea

questions.solution_md: Sunbeam → Tyndall; jiggling → Brownian; drifting → electrophoresis; delta → coagulation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A lyophobic sol is coagulated by adding a small amount of electrolyte.

**Reason (R):** The ions of opposite charge neutralise the charge on the colloidal particles, which then aggregate.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Brownian movement helps keep colloidal particles from settling.

**Reason (R):** Colloidal particles are too heavy to be moved by molecules of the dispersion medium.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — the particles are small enough to be knocked about by unequal bombardment from medium molecules — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** NaCl coagulates a positively charged ferric hydroxide sol more effectively than Na₂SO₄.

**Reason (R):** For a positively charged sol, the coagulating power of an anion increases with the magnitude of its charge.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: SO₄²⁻ (charge 2−) is a stronger coagulant than Cl⁻ for a positive sol, which is exactly what R (a true statement of the Hardy–Schulze rule) predicts — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A sol needs 52 mmol L⁻¹ of NaCl but only 0.65 mmol L⁻¹ of BaCl₂ for coagulation. How many times greater is the coagulating power of BaCl₂ than that of NaCl? (Coagulating power is inversely proportional to coagulation value.)
A colloidal gold particle has a diameter of 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m. What is its diameter in nanometres?
questions.solution_md: $1\ \text{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \text{m}$; diameter $= 2.5 \times 10^{-8} \div 10^{-9} = 25$, so $25\ \text{nm}$ (within the colloidal range).

questions.stem_md: Give two differences between lyophilic and lyophobic sols, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Lyophilic sols, such as starch in water, have strong affinity between particles and medium, form simply by mixing, and are reversible and stable. Lyophobic sols, such as gold or arsenious sulfide in water, have little affinity, need special methods to prepare, are irreversible, and are coagulated by small amounts of electrolyte.

questions.solution_md: Affinity, preparation, reversibility, stability; examples.

questions.stem_md: Oil and vinegar salad dressing separates on standing, but mayonnaise, which also contains egg yolk, does not. Explain, and say what type of emulsion mayonnaise is.

answer.model_answer_md: Oil and vinegar are immiscible, so droplets formed by shaking soon join up and the layers separate. Egg yolk contains proteins and lecithin that act as an emulsifying agent, forming a film around the oil droplets and keeping them apart. Mayonnaise is an oil-in-water emulsion.

questions.solution_md: Emulsifier from egg yolk; O/W.

marking_scheme.step: Egg yolk acts as an emulsifying agent

questions.stem_md: Explain how a ferric hydroxide sol acquires a positive charge and why this charge keeps the sol stable.

answer.model_answer_md: When FeCl₃ is hydrolysed in hot water, the hydrated ferric oxide particles preferentially adsorb Fe³⁺ ions, which are common to them, so they become positively charged and are surrounded by a layer of Cl⁻ ions. Since every particle carries the same positive charge, the particles repel one another and cannot come together to form larger particles that would settle.

questions.solution_md: Preferential adsorption of Fe³⁺; mutual repulsion.

questions.stem_md: In a village, muddy river water is purified by stirring in a little potash alum and leaving it to stand. Explain the chemistry.

answer.model_answer_md: The fine clay particles in muddy water form a negatively charged colloid that does not settle. Alum supplies Al³⁺ ions, whose high positive charge neutralises the charge on the clay particles (Hardy–Schulze rule). The neutral particles aggregate and settle, leaving clearer water above.

questions.solution_md: Al³⁺ coagulates negative clay sol.

marking_scheme.step: Clay is a negatively charged colloid
Al³⁺ neutralises charge; particles coagulate and settle

questions.stem_md: Three liquids are tested: salt water, starch solution and muddy water. Predict, with reasons, how each behaves (a) when filtered through filter paper, (b) on standing for a day, and (c) when a narrow beam of light is passed through it.

answer.model_answer_md: Salt water is a true solution with particles smaller than 1 nm: it passes through filter paper, does not settle and shows no Tyndall effect. Starch solution is a colloid with particles of 1–1000 nm: it passes through filter paper, does not settle, but scatters light so the beam is visible. Muddy water is a suspension with particles larger than 1000 nm: the mud is held back by filter paper and settles on standing; the cloudy liquid also scatters light.

questions.solution_md: True solution, colloid, suspension.

questions.stem_md: State the Hardy–Schulze rule. Arrange (a) NaCl, AlCl₃, MgCl₂ for coagulating an arsenious sulfide sol and (b) KCl, K₂SO₄, K₃[Fe(CN)₆] for coagulating a ferric hydroxide sol, in decreasing order of coagulating power.

answer.model_answer_md: Hardy–Schulze rule: the ion carrying a charge opposite to that of the sol particles causes coagulation, and the greater the charge on that ion, the greater its coagulating power. (a) Arsenious sulfide is a negative sol, so cations act: AlCl₃ > MgCl₂ > NaCl. (b) Ferric hydroxide is a positive sol, so anions act: K₃[Fe(CN)₆] > K₂SO₄ > KCl.

questions.solution_md: Rule; cations for negative sol; anions for positive sol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between true solutions, colloids and suspensions on the basis of particle size and two other properties.

(b) Classify colloids on the basis of the physical state of the phases, giving four examples.

(c) What are associated colloids? Explain the formation of micelles.

answer.model_answer_md: In a true solution particles are smaller than 1 nm, in a colloid 1–1000 nm, and in a suspension larger than 1000 nm. True solutions and colloids pass through filter paper, but suspensions do not; colloids and suspensions scatter light, but true solutions do not; suspensions settle on standing. A colloid has a dispersed phase in a dispersion medium: solid in liquid gives a sol (paint), liquid in gas an aerosol (fog), liquid in liquid an emulsion (milk), and gas in liquid a foam (lather). Associated colloids behave as normal electrolytes at low concentration but form aggregated particles at higher concentration. Soap anions, RCOO⁻, have a long non-polar tail and a polar head. Above the critical micelle concentration and Kraft temperature, they cluster with tails inward and heads outward, forming spherical micelles of colloidal size.

questions.solution_md: Size and properties; phases with examples; micelles.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain the Tyndall effect and Brownian movement.

(b) How do colloidal particles acquire charge? How is the sign of the charge found?

(c) What is coagulation? Give three ways of coagulating a lyophobic sol and explain how lyophilic colloids protect lyophobic sols.

answer.model_answer_md: When light passes through a sol, colloidal particles scatter it, so the path of the beam is visible from the side; this is the Tyndall effect. Under a microscope, colloidal particles move in zigzag paths because molecules of the medium strike them unequally; this is Brownian movement. Particles acquire charge mainly by preferential adsorption of ions common to them, such as Fe³⁺ on ferric hydroxide. In electrophoresis, the sol is placed in an electric field; the direction in which the particles move shows their charge. Coagulation is the aggregation and settling of colloidal particles when their charge is neutralised. It can be caused by adding electrolytes, by electrophoresis, by mixing oppositely charged sols, or by boiling. A lyophilic colloid forms a protective solvated layer around the lyophobic particles, preventing their coagulation.

questions.solution_md: Tyndall, Brownian; charge and electrophoresis; coagulation and protection.

questions.stem_md: Use ideas from colloid chemistry to explain: (a) the formation of a delta at a river mouth; (b) how a Cottrell precipitator cleans chimney smoke; (c) why the sky appears blue; (d) how soap removes oily dirt from cloth; (e) why gelatin is added when making ice cream.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) River water carries negatively charged colloidal clay; electrolytes in sea water neutralise the charge, so the clay coagulates and settles, building a delta. (b) Smoke contains charged carbon particles; in the precipitator they pass between highly charged electrodes, lose their charge, coagulate and fall, while clean gas escapes. (c) Dust and water droplets of colloidal size in the air scatter blue light more than red, so scattered light from the sky looks blue. (d) Soap anions form micelles: their hydrocarbon tails dissolve in the grease and their charged heads face the water, so oily dirt is emulsified and washed away. (e) Gelatin is a protective lyophilic colloid; it coats fine particles and stops ice crystals and fat separating, keeping ice cream smooth.

questions.passage_md: A student studies the adsorption of nitrogen on a sample of silica at 77 K and records the mass adsorbed per gram (x/m) at different pressures. Plotting log(x/m) against log p gives a straight line of slope 0.50 and intercept −0.30. At a much higher temperature the adsorption becomes very small. In another experiment, hydrogen on nickel is adsorbed more at 400 K than at 200 K. (log 2 = 0.30)

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) 2

**(b)** 0.5

**(c)** (i) Nitrogen on silica is physisorbed by weak van der Waals forces; this exothermic process decreases as temperature rises. Hydrogen on nickel is chemisorbed (Ni–H bonds form); chemisorption needs activation energy, so its extent increases with temperature over this range.

**OR** (ii) x/m = k p^(1/n) = 0.5 × 4^0.5 = 0.5 × 2 = 1.0. The Freundlich isotherm is empirical and holds only over a limited range of pressure; at high pressure x/m approaches a limit and the equation fails.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Slope = 1/n = 0.50, so n = 2 — option (c).

**(b)** $\log k = -0.30$, so $k = 10^{-0.30} = 1 \div 2 = 0.5$.

**(c)** (i) Physisorption vs activated chemisorption.

(ii) x/m = 1.0; limited pressure range.
